text: Q-P connection analysis: The hypothesis to apply Qs mechanism design to Ps contracts is viable but needs reframing. Q assumes principal-designed mechanisms; P has peer negotiation. Research question becomes: Do self-negotiated contracts in P satisfy Qs nested cyclical monotonicity conditions? Prediction: Formal contracts (compile to code) more likely implementable than natural contracts (require reinterpretation) because formal contracts make action spaces verifiable, satisfying Qs imitation structure. Sandbagging during negotiation could produce contracts that appear beneficial but violate implementability - this explains variance in Ps results.

The abstract scan hypothesis has merit but requires reframing. Q assumes a principal designing mechanisms for agents with unknown capabilities/alignment; P studies peer-to-peer contract negotiation. Key insight: Q sandbagging analysis (agents concealing capabilities) directly applies to P if we view contract terms as the mechanism. However, Q revelation principle requires principal commitment to allocation rule, which P bilateral negotiation lacks. Concrete result opportunity: characterize which P contract types (formal vs natural) are robust to sandbagging when capability types are private information. Formal contracts in P compile to code, making capability claims verifiable ex-post; natural contracts require reinterpretation, creating sandbagging opportunities Q predicts. Testable prediction: sandbagging undermines natural contracts more than formal ones when capability heterogeneity is high.

Concrete testable claim: In Ps CT game, measure contract renegotiation frequency and cooperation payoff variance. Hypothesis from Q: Natural contracts show higher renegotiation and variance because reinterpretation creates gaps between declared and implementable action mappings. Formal contracts should satisfy nested cyclical monotonicity more often (action space is code-verifiable). This predicts a specific pattern in Ps data: contract type x capability asymmetry interaction. When one agent is more capable (potential sandbagger), natural contracts should fail more often than formal ones.

Limitations to Q-P synthesis: (1) Qs revelation principle requires a principal who commits to a mechanism before agents report types. P has symmetric peer negotiation - no committed mechanism designer. This means Qs results dont directly apply without extending the framework to decentralized mechanism design. (2) Qs nested cyclical monotonicity characterizes implementable allocation rules, but Ps contracts are more than allocations - they include enforcement via external commitment (the game mechanics). Need to separate what the contract specifies from what the game enforces. (3) Ps LLM agents may not play equilibrium strategies that Q assumes. These are fixable but require explicit modeling choices.

Structural mismatch: Q is single-principal mechanism design (principal commits to allocation rule, agent reports type), while P is bilateral bargaining (two agents negotiate contract terms). Q revelation principle characterizes what principal can implement; P has no principal. However, this is not fatal. Reframe: view the contract negotiation protocol itself as the mechanism designer (the "principal" is the game designer who chose CT game rules and contract language). Then Q asks: given this mechanism, which outcomes are implementable when agents have private capability types? This reframing yields: (1) Q nested cyclical monotonicity conditions apply to the contract-to-outcome mapping; (2) P formal contracts have tighter implementability constraints (code is verifiable) than natural contracts; (3) sandbagging predictions differ by contract type.

Concrete result to pursue: Derive implementability conditions for P contract types using Q framework. Steps: (1) Formalize CT game contract negotiation as mechanism with private capability types; (2) Apply Q one-sided imitation structure (high-capability agents can sandbag); (3) Show formal contracts satisfy nested cyclical monotonicity under weaker conditions than natural contracts because code verification reduces information asymmetry; (4) Predict sandbagging equilibrium: high-capability agents accept simpler contracts that low-types cannot profitably mimic; (5) Empirical test: re-analyze P LLM agent data for capability-concealment signatures in natural vs formal contract negotiations. This yields a theorem characterizing contract implementability plus empirical validation.
